summary: Module 2 REFLECT (Decomposition). The 60/40 lesson landed: decomposition is the highest-leverage skill, and its real content is interface contracts, not splitting. Concrete learnings: (1) My one-sentence spec 'add team invitations' hid six subtasks -- data model, send endpoint, email, acceptance flow, expiry, revocation -- plus an edge-case matrix (dup invite, already-member, inviter-loses-admin, token replay, expiry race). Naming them before prompting is what makes prompts atomic: acceptance criteria stateable in two sentences. (2) Task 1 (data model) built the rich schema: teams.created_by owner + team_members join table with roles + invitations. (3) The BREAK exposed my own decomposition bug: Task 2's prompt was written from my ORIGINAL PLAN (teams.owner_id, flat membership) not from Task 1's actual output -- the exact failure the module teaches. The agent silently adapted; the lesson is that a literal agent would have produced code that would not compile. (4) FIX: interface contracts make conflicts visible BEFORE running prompts. Writing Task 1's actual output (exact tables, columns, roles, permission rules, error semantics) into Task 2's prompt eliminated all divergence -- corrected re-run found zero deviations and all 7 acceptance criteria verified live. (5) Preventative rule adopted: every post-Task-1 prompt embeds the upstream task's ACTUAL output; schema divergence found at review means fix the prompt, never silently patch code. Decisions recorded: decomposition_approach = top_down first pass refined progressively; task_granularity = medium (8-12 tasks, 50-150 lines) -- matching the module's 150-line cap and my M1 cost-asymmetry reasoning.
